newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU watches -- again -- while Albania flares.
newsitem.headline: EU watches -- again -- while Albania flares.

text.p: Faced with the nightmare prospect of major unrest in the Balkans, European states struggled on Tuesday to find a common stand over how to react to worsening events in Albania.
With the tiny, impoverished country in turmoil, diplomats said EU countries were in danger of once again appearing to sit back and watch while violence spreads in Europe's backyard.

The Albanian parliament has declared a state of emergency and the government of President Sali Berisha issued orders to shoot armed rioters on sight and imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew after parliament declared a state of emergency.
But several days into the crisis, the current Dutch presidency has failed to issue even a statement.
"The Netherlands is in close contact with other states, but so far there has been no agreement on what to put out," one diplomat said.

The inaction carried uneasy reminders of the EU's failure to stop the wars in former Yugoslavia and prevent NATO allies Greece and Turkey almost coming to blows over a disputed islet in the Aegean last year.
On both occasions, a more muscular U.S. diplomacy stepped into the breach, prompting Europeans to bridle at suggestions they were incapable of crisis management on their own continent.

So far the only official EU reaction has been a statement by European External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek urging restraint on all sides -- a wish that appeared to have been overtaken by events even before it was expressed.

"The situation is extremely worrying and the European Union will certainly urge President Berisha -- but also the opposition -- to show restraint, not to use violence and to try and solve this serious crisis by peaceful means," van den Broek said in Moscow on Monday.

On Thursday, senior officials from EU countries are set to meet in Brussels to discuss what measures the Union, which has pumped some 400 million European currency units into the country in recent years, could take.
A Commission spokesman said on Tuesday it was for EU member states, not the bloc's executive arm, to decide what to do.

"They could suspend aid projects, but that hits the people we are trying to help," the spokesman said, adding that the Commission was drawing up plans to evacuate several dozen staff working on projects in the country.

Meanwhile on Tuesday, as Albanian troops enforced emergency rule in Europe's poorest country, Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu defended the emergency measures, saying they had succeeded in pulling the mountainous state back from the brink of civil war.

"With this ruling the risk of civil war has diminished hugely. If we had not taken it, do you know what would have happened? That today Tirana would have been attacked by the rebels," Shehu told Italy's leftist daily L'Unita.
He said the south was "completely out of control".
The EU's silence was once again in sharp contrast to the expressions of alarm coming out of Washington.

"We're very concerned that the state of emergency declared by the parliament today is being used to stifle legitimate free expression," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.
Burns sharply criticised the election of Berisha on Monday to a second five-year term.
Diplomats fear a complete breakdown in the tiny Balkan country of just over three million people could have serious implications for what is already an unstable region.

They said there were two major concerns beyond the immediate loss of life in Albania itself -- the risk that hundreds of thousands of refugees may pour into Greece or across the sea to Italy, and the risk of sparking wider unrest among ethnic Albanians in neighbouring countries.
Diplomats and analysts fear unrest in Albania could reignite the Balkans by drawing in ethnic Albanians living in the Kosovo region of Serbia and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
These are already highly sensitive areas, with unresolved ethnic and minority problems despite the end of the war in former Yugoslavia.
